If you already build plots with **ggplot2** or **ggpubr**, you don't need to learn a new plotting
API to make them interactive. [canvasXpress](https://canvasxpress.org) accepts a **ggplot object
directly**: pass it to `canvasXpress()` and it renders an interactive, reproducible version of the
same figure — you keep your existing code.

## Install

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages(c("canvasXpress", "ggpubr"))
```

## Wrap a plot you already have

Here's an ordinary `ggpubr` boxplot with **pairwise comparisons** (`geom_pwc`) — the significance
brackets that show a test between each pair of groups. Build it exactly as you normally would:

```{r}
#| message: false
library(ggplot2)
library(ggpubr)

g <- ggboxplot(iris, x = "Species", y = "Sepal.Width", fill = "Species") +
  geom_pwc(method = "t_test", label = "p.format")
```

Now make it interactive — **one call, the same object**:

```{r}
#| message: false
library(canvasXpress)

canvasXpress(g)
```

That's the whole idea: no re-specification. canvasXpress reads the ggplot object — its data,
aesthetics, layers, scales and the `geom_pwc` brackets — and renders it. Hover the points, drag to
zoom, or open the toolbar to filter and re-style, and the result serializes to one portable spec you
can store and reproduce from R, Python or JavaScript.

## What transfers

- **Geoms and layers** — points, boxes, lines, and stats like `geom_pwc` / `stat_compare_means`.
- **Aesthetic mappings** — `x`, `y`, `fill`, `color`, grouping.
- **Scales, labels and facets** from the ggplot object.

## When to reach for the native API instead

Wrapping a ggplot is ideal for reusing plots you already have. When you're building a figure fresh —
or want fine control over CanvasXpress-specific features (clustering, dendrograms, interactive
annotations) — call `canvasXpress()` on your data directly with a `graphType`. See the other posts
for that style.
